analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour over five years and ends lower minimums for tipped workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 37 of 48 Senate Democrats cosponsoring, the bill was referred to committee the day it arrived and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps from $9.50 to $15 an hour over five years, then adjust it each year with the growth in the national median wage. It would also phase out the separate, lower minimum wages for tipped workers, for newly hired teenagers, and for some workers with disabilities, so all three groups would eventually be covered by the full minimum wage. The bill was introduced on January 26, 2021 and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it stayed for the rest of the two-year Congress without a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum, including the roughly two million people who work for tips and workers with disabilities now paid below the minimum under special certificates. Tipped workers currently can be paid as little as $2.13 an hour in cash wages; under the bill, their cash wage rises each year until it equals the full minimum wage, and they keep the legal right to retain their tips. Workers with disabilities under subminimum certificates would move up a fixed ladder to $15 and the certificates would expire.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum wage in annual steps: $9.50 on enactment, then $11, $12.50, $14, and $15 at one-year intervals, with automatic increases after that tied to growth in the median hourly wage of all employees.

Phases out the separate tipped minimum wage: the required cash wage for tipped employees rises $2 an hour each year until it reaches the full minimum wage, and employees get an explicit right to retain their tips.

Ends the subminimum wage for workers with disabilities: their wages rise on a five-year schedule to the full minimum, no new subminimum certificates may be issued, and existing certificates lose legal effect once the final increase takes effect.
Phases out the lower minimum for newly hired workers under 20 on a similar schedule, then repeals that provision entirely.
Requires the Labor Department to publish each wage increase in the Federal Register and online 60 days before it takes effect, so employers and workers get advance notice.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay below the new wage floors, most directly restaurants that rely on the $2.13 tipped minimum and employers holding special certificates to pay workers with disabilities subminimum wages. The five-year phase-in is designed to spread the payroll increase over time.

drawbacks.text: The bill puts employers on a fixed five-year schedule to eliminate every lower wage tier, including the tipped minimum and the youth training wage, with no adjustment mechanism if their business conditions change.

The strongest good-faith objection is that raising a wage floor raises payroll costs, and critics warn some low-margin employers respond by cutting hours, raising prices, or eliminating jobs; the bill's answer is the long phase-in and a requirement that the Labor Department provide transition assistance to certificate-holding employers and help ensure continuing employment for workers with disabilities.

For some workers with disabilities employed under subminimum-wage certificates, the transition to the full minimum could mean the end of the segregated jobs they currently hold, which is why the bill directs Labor to provide referrals to competitive integrated employment programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains run to millions of workers at the bottom of the wage scale, including groups that have been legally excluded from the full minimum wage for decades, and the five-year phase-in gives employers room to adjust. The honest cost is higher payroll bills for low-wage employers and real uncertainty for sheltered-workshop employment of workers with disabilities, which the bill tries to soften with transition assistance but cannot fully offset. On the question of job losses, the record in these sources does not settle it; the phase-in design reflects an attempt to limit that risk.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on January 26, 2021 by Senator Sanders along with 38 other senators, including the Democratic leader Chuck Schumer.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
37 senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill, but that is the last action in the bill's history: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action before the Congress ended.
The separate minimum wage for tipped workers, the youth subminimum, and the disability subminimum all remained in federal law because the bill never passed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay below $15 an hour are better off because the bill never moved: restaurants that use the tipped minimum wage keep paying a lower cash wage, and employers holding special certificates keep paying workers with disabilities below the minimum, since none of the phase-outs ever took effect.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with 38 Senate cosponsors and led the push for a $15 federal minimum wage.

for.name: 37 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it the near-unanimous position of the Senate Democratic caucus.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction but never brought it to the Senate floor for a vote.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, but her committee never held a markup or advanced it after the referral.

against.name: Kyrsten Sinema
against.what_they_did: Voted to strip the $15 minimum wage from the COVID-19 relief bill in March 2021, closing the Senate's main alternative route to enacting it that year.

against.name: Joe Manchin
against.what_they_did: Opposed including the $15 minimum wage in the COVID-19 relief bill and voted to remove it from that measure, siding with Republicans on the procedural fight.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed any $15 federal minimum wage; no Republican cosponsored this bill and the caucus's opposition meant it could never reach 60 votes on the floor, so it was never brought to a vote.

against.name: Elizabeth MacDonough
against.what_they_did: Ruled in February 2021 that a $15 minimum wage could not be included in the budget reconciliation bill Democrats were using to pass COVID-19 relief without 60 votes, removing the one path around Republican opposition.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were Senate Democrats and no Republican signed on; the fight over a $15 wage in 2021 split almost entirely by party, with a small handful of Democrats breaking from their caucus on the alternative route through the relief bill.

industries.note: Restaurants are the largest users of the $2.13 tipped minimum wage; the bill phases their required cash wage up to the full $15 minimum within five years and explicitly guarantees employees keep their tips. Their interest in keeping the lower cash wage runs directly against the wages of the workers they employ.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and holders of subminimum-wage certificates for workers with disabilities
industries.note: The bill raises their workers' pay on a five-year ladder to $15, bars any new subminimum certificates, and sunsets all existing ones. These employers' ability to pay less than the minimum wage is exactly what workers with disabilities would gain back.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers generally (retail, food service, childcare, home care)
industries.note: Businesses paying between $7.25 and $15 an hour face a rising payroll floor on a fixed schedule. Cheaper labor is the thing their workers would be paid instead.
